0.0.n: The adverb form of 早い describes how promptly the speaker needs to leave.

0.1.n: Casual shortening of 行かなければならない, expressing necessity; the ending meaning “won’t do” is left unsaid.

1.0.n: A borrowed clothing word; Japanese leaves “my” unstated here.

1.1.n: Marks the jacket as the thing being put on.

1.2.n: The て-form of 着る links putting on upper-body clothing to the next action.

2.0.n: This noun comes before の to identify which item the zipper belongs to.

2.1.n: Links ジャケット to ファスナー, showing that the zipper is part of the jacket.

2.2.n: This borrowed word refers to the jacket’s fastening mechanism.

2.3.n: Marks the zipper as the thing being closed.

2.4.n: Polite form of 閉める, meaning to close something; with a zipper, English uses “zip up.”

3.0.n: This borrowed noun names the location where the tissues are.

3.1.n: Marks the pocket as the location where something exists.

3.2.n: Makes the pocket’s location the topic, potentially contrasting it with other places.

3.3.n: Japanese nouns do not normally mark singular or plural; the context supplies the number.

3.4.n: Identifies the tissues as the things that are present.

3.5.n: Polite form of ある, used for the existence of things rather than people or animals.

4.0.n: Names the items being identified; the subject is understood from context.

4.1.n: A polite sentence ending used here to identify what the items are.

5.0.n: Refers back to the items in the pocket.

5.1.n: Marks the tissues as the things the speaker will take along.

5.2.n: 持って, the て-form of 持つ, combines with polite 行きます to describe taking something when going somewhere.

0.tip: なきゃ is a casual way to say you have to do something.

1.tip: The て-form connects this action to the next instead of finishing the sentence.

2.tip: 閉める means to close something, including zippers.

3.lit: As for in the pocket, tissues exist.
3.tip: には combines the location marker に with は to make that location the topic.

4.tip: Japanese often omits the subject when it is clear from context.

5.tip: 持って行く means taking something along when you go, rather than merely holding it.
